title: Browser launch-token authentication
summary: The host authenticates every API call before dispatch. It creates a random token at launch, the browser exchanges it once for a signed cookie, and the Host and Origin checks still run first.
firstReason: A loopback Host header is not proof of local authority, so token authentication is required for the Go server as well.

title: Web app-owned routes are document-relative
summary: The served page declares one base element and every browser reference to an application route is relative to the document, so the application works behind a proxy that mounts it under a path prefix.
firstReason: Server-rendered pages and htmx requests need the same rule to work behind a prefix-stripping proxy; keep it.

title: Bind one concrete Web address
summary: The web listener binds exactly one concrete IPv4 or IPv6 address, loopback by default, and rejects wildcard addresses such as 0.0.0.0. The Host-header check accepts the bind address itself; any other name must be listed as a trusted host.
firstReason: A wildcard bind exposed every interface and made the host infer trust from sampled LAN addresses. One explicit address keeps configured trust and actual reachability the same thing, which matters equally for a Go listener.

title: Native HTTPS on the Web listener
summary: The web listener can serve HTTPS itself from a certificate file and a key file. Invalid or mismatched key material fails start-up with no fallback to HTTP, and the listener's actual protocol, not forwarded headers, decides the `Secure` cookie attribute.
firstReason: A directly reached listener must be able to encrypt launch tokens and cookies without a reverse proxy. Go's standard library serves TLS directly; the fail-closed rule and the rule that TLS grants no extra authority carry unchanged.

title: Session-log OTLP strings and bounded requests
summary: Session-log telemetry goes through a shared telemetry (OTLP) plugin with its own queue bounded by bytes and by count. Each record is measured once after serialization; one oversized record is reported and skipped without blocking later ones.
firstReason: Count-only batching cannot bound a request once large tool results are JSON-escaped. Byte-bounded batching, and the rule that one bad record does not block the queue, apply to a Go exporter as well.
